title: If one microservice is down, how do you handle it gracefully (circuit breaker, fallback, retry with backoff, timeout, bulkhead, graceful degradation, monitoring)?
shortTitle: If one microservice is down, how do you handle it gracefully
keyPoints: A timeout on every remote call is the first and most important defense against a hanging dependency
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter gives transient failures a second chance without stampeding
A circuit breaker fails fast once failures are sustained, protecting both caller and callee
A fallback provides a degraded but useful response such as a cached value or a safe default
A bulkhead isolates resources so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all threads and sink the whole service
Monitoring and alerting on breaker state, retry counts, and timeout rates close the loop for operators
Only retry idempotent operations to avoid double-charging the customer

s1_definition.oneliner: When a dependency is down, fail fast with a timeout, retry transient errors with backoff, trip a circuit breaker to stop the bleeding, and serve a fallback so the user still gets a useful answer.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Timeout** – every remote call has a bounded wait so a hanging dependency never ties up threads indefinitely.
- **Retry with backoff** – the caller retries a bounded number of times with growing delays and jitter, absorbing transient blips.
- **Circuit breaker** – once failures cross a threshold the breaker opens and fails instantly, protecting both caller and callee.
- **Fallback** – when the primary path fails, a degraded but useful response such as a cached value or default is returned.
- **Bulkhead** – limits concurrent calls per dependency so one slow service cannot exhaust all threads.
- **Graceful degradation** – the system continues to provide core value with reduced functionality rather than failing completely.
- **Monitoring** – circuit breaker state, retry counts, and timeout rates emit metrics and alerts to close the loop.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India's branch depends on a central credit-score office to approve loans. One day the credit office phone line is dead. A graceful teller does not keep Rajesh waiting at the counter forever (that is a timeout), does not redial frantically hundreds of times (that is retry with backoff), and after noticing the line has been dead for a while, stops dialing altogether for a few minutes to save effort (that is a circuit breaker). Instead the teller tells Rajesh "we will give you a provisional decision based on your existing relationship" (that is a fallback and graceful degradation) and quietly files a report so the manager knows the line is down (that is monitoring).

sections.s6_takeaway:
When one microservice is down, the goal is to contain the blast radius so the caller stays responsive and the failure does not cascade. The toolkit is layered: a timeout on every remote call as the first defense, because the worst failure is not an error but a call that hangs forever and ties up threads. On top of timeouts, retry with exponential backoff and jitter gives transient blips a second chance, but only for idempotent operations. Then a circuit breaker watches the failure rate and opens when failures are sustained, so subsequent calls fail instantly without touching the network.

The piece that keeps customers served is the fallback. When the fraud-check service went down at National Bank of India, instead of rejecting every transfer, the fallback applied a conservative default risk score for low-value transfers and flagged them for later manual review, so legitimate customers like Rajesh were still served while high-risk cases stayed protected. Bulkheads cap how many concurrent calls a single dependency can consume, so if statement generation becomes slow it cannot starve the threads that handle transfers.

None of this is complete without monitoring and alerting. Circuit breaker state changes, retry counts, timeout rates, and fallback invocations all emit metrics to Prometheus, and we alert the on-call engineer when the breaker opens or the fallback rate spikes, because a silent fallback that quietly masks an outage for days is its own failure.

Remember one sentence: fail fast with timeouts, retry transient errors with backoff, trip a circuit breaker to stop the bleeding, serve a fallback so the user still gets a useful answer, isolate with bulkheads, and watch everything with metrics and alerts.
